intro: Long ago, in many parts of the world, the family you were born into set your place in life. A king's child grew up to rule. A farmer's child grew up to farm. In this unit you will visit castles in England, samurai in Japan, scholars in China, and rulers of the Aztec and Inca.

Then you will come to today. You will learn words like income, wealth and opportunity. You will see why some people and countries have more than others. You will also meet the neighbors, libraries and food banks that help.

By the end, you will be able to explain how ranks by birth worked and how they changed. You will be able to name reasons people have more or less. And you will be able to share your own idea about what makes a chance fair, using facts.
bigQuestion: How did being rich or poor work long ago, how does it work now, and what makes a fair chance?

timeline.t: Confucius teaches in China about family, learning and good behavior
English nobles make King John agree to Magna Carta
English peasants march to London in the Peasants' Revolt
The Aztec and Inca empires are at their largest
Japan's rulers sort people into ranks, with samurai at the top
China ends its old civil service exams
The United Nations says everyone has the right to education
World Bank: fewer than 1 in 10 people live in extreme poverty

words.d: a person's place in a group, from high to low
a way of sorting people into ranks, like steps on a ladder
a king or queen who rules a country
a member of a powerful family with land and a title
a peasant tied to a lord's land who could not leave without permission
a warrior in Japan who served a lord and was born into that rank
money that comes in over time, like pay from a job
everything a person owns, minus what they owe
something you own that has value, like a home or a business
a group that helps people and does not try to make a profit
money people and businesses pay to the government for shared services
a real chance to do something, like go to school or get a job

test.q: Long ago in many places, what mostly decided a person's rank?
choices: The family they were born into
test.why: In many places long ago, rank came from the family you were born into.

test.q: Which word means a peasant tied to a lord's land?
test.why: A serf was tied to a lord's land.

choices: A lord's land with fields, a mill and a village
test.why: A manor was a lord's land and village together.

test.q: Which group chose many officials with hard written tests?
test.why: China used civil service exams to choose officials.

test.q: How were Japan's merchants and samurai different from about 1600 to the 1860s?
choices: Samurai ranked higher, but some merchants were richer
test.why: Samurai ranked at the top, but some low-ranked merchants became very rich.

test.q: What was mit'a in the Inca Empire?
choices: A duty to take turns working for the state
test.why: Mit'a was the Inca duty of taking turns working for the state.

test.q: Why did the Black Death give peasants more power?
choices: It left fewer workers, so their work was needed more
test.why: With far fewer workers, lords needed the peasants who survived.

choices: Even the king must follow the law
test.why: Magna Carta said even the king had to follow the law.

test.q: What is the difference between income and wealth?
choices: Wealth is only pay from a job
Income is money coming in; wealth is all you own minus what you owe
Income is a house; wealth is a paycheck
test.why: Income comes in over time; wealth is what you own minus what you owe.

test.q: What does the Bureau of Labor Statistics chart show about school and pay?
choices: More schooling goes with higher pay, on average
Less schooling always means higher pay
test.why: The chart shows typical weekly pay rising with more schooling.

test.q: Which is an example of luck changing a family's money?
test.why: A storm happens by chance, not by choice, so it is luck.

test.q: What does the unit say being poor tells you about a person?
choices: It does not tell you who they are
That they will always be poor
test.why: Being poor has many causes and says nothing about a person's worth.

test.q: How are public libraries and schools in the U.S. paid for?
choices: By a fee at the door
test.why: Public libraries and schools are paid for by taxes.

test.q: What happened to the share of people in extreme poverty from 1990 to 2019, according to the World Bank?
choices: It fell from more than 1 in 3 to fewer than 1 in 10
test.why: World Bank estimates show a drop from about 38 percent to about 9 percent.

test.q: People disagree about who should help families in need. Which answer describes the unit's view?
choices: People debate the mix, and most countries use several kinds of help
test.why: The unit says each view has supporters and critics, and most countries use a mix.

write.prompt: Is it fairer today than long ago for a child to choose their own path in life? Make a claim. Use two or three facts from the unit, like serfdom, the Peasants' Revolt, public libraries or the World Bank numbers, to explain it.
tips: Start with one clear sentence that says your claim.
Name where each fact comes from, like the World Bank or Magna Carta.
Give one reason someone might see it differently.
Use unit words like rank, opportunity and wealth.
